title: 1. Biology of the Neocortex
intro: Before building a cortical column in a simulator or on a chip, it helps to know what the biological one is made of: six layers with distinct inputs and outputs, repeated vertical units at two scales, a small number of cell classes with stereotyped wiring, constant dialogue with the thalamus, and the bold idea that the whole cortex runs one algorithm. This section gives you those facts with numbers attached, and says on every page which details to keep and which to abstract away.

blocks.text: Every computational column model — HTM, the Thousand Brains framework, the Potjans–Diesmann microcircuit, Diehl & Cook-style STDP networks — is a compression of the same biology. Knowing the original lets you see what each model kept and what it dropped, and lets you make those choices deliberately in your own model. It also gives you sanity checks: firing rates, cell proportions, connection probabilities and time constants that a plausible spiking column should roughly reproduce.

A caution that runs through the whole section: many textbook numbers (100 neurons per minicolumn, 80% excitatory cells, six layers everywhere) are good orders of magnitude but vary by species, area and measurement method. The pages give ranges and flag the debated points. When a model result depends on one of these numbers, sweep it.
Pages in this section, in learning order

items: Cortical Layers L1–L6: what each layer receives and sends — L4 thalamic input, L2/3 cortico-cortical, L5 subcortical output, L6 thalamic feedback, L1 apical tufts and top-down input — and how agranular areas differ.
Minicolumns and Columns: the roughly 100-neuron minicolumn versus the 300–600 µm macrocolumn, barrel cortex as the clearest case, and the Horton & Adams (2005) critique.
Cell Types: pyramidal and spiny stellate excitatory cells; PV, SST and VIP interneurons and their motifs, including VIP → SST disinhibition.
Thalamocortical Loops: drivers versus modulators, core versus matrix, first-order versus higher-order thalamus, the L6 feedback loop and the L5 transthalamic pathway.
Mountcastle's Hypothesis: the common cortical algorithm, the ferret rewiring evidence, and the counter-evidence that areas are tuned differently.

blocks.text: How this connects to the rest of the topic

items: Section 2 (Spiking Neuron Models) turns the cell types here into equations: LIF and Izhikevich for point neurons, active dendrites for pyramidal cells.
Section 3 (Plasticity and Learning) covers how these circuits learn; the inhibitory motifs here are the biological basis of k-WTA and sparse codes.
Sections 4 and 5 (HTM and Thousand Brains) use the minicolumn, the layer roles and Mountcastle's hypothesis as explicit design premises.
Section 6 (Other Column Models) shows data-driven circuits (Potjans–Diesmann, Blue Brain) that encode the layer and cell-type statistics from this section directly.
A practical column model needs at least L4 (input), L2/3 (lateral and cortico-cortical), L5 (output) and L6 (feedback to the input stage), each with its own inhibition.
'Column' means two different things: a minicolumn (~80–120 neurons, ~30–60 µm) or a macrocolumn (~10⁴ neurons, ~300–600 µm). Say which one you mean.
About 70–85% of neurons are excitatory. Sparse, weak E → E connectivity plus dense, fast PV inhibition gives stable, sparse activity; SST gates dendrites; VIP disinhibits.
Separate driving inputs (which define what a neuron represents) from modulating inputs (which set gain and gating). Thalamic and cortical feedback are mostly modulatory.
The common-algorithm hypothesis is a productive working assumption, not a proven fact: areas share a circuit template but differ in parameters.
